# Introduction

The following document provides a hands-on tutorial on discrete and continuous
CDFs using partial moments and an extension to ANOVA analysis.

## Install NNS

We need the latest version of NNS available on GitHub.

```{r install}
#require(devtools); install_github('OVVO-Financial/NNS', ref = "NNS-Beta-Version")
library(NNS)
```

# CDFs

Cumulative distribution functions (CDFs) represent the probability a variable
$X$ will take a value less than or equal to $x$.

$$F(x) = P(X \le x)$$

## Empirical CDF

The empirical CDF is a simple construct, provided in the base package of R. We
can generate an empirical CDF with the `ecdf` function and create a function
(`P`) to return the CDF of a given value of $X$.

```{r ecdf}
set.seed(123); x = rnorm(100)
ecdf(x)
P = ecdf(x)
P(0); P(1)
```

### Lower Partial Moment CDF (LPM.CDF)

The empirical CDF and Lower Partial Moment CDF (LPM.CDF) are identical when the
degree term of the LPM.CDF is set to zero.

Using the same targets from our `ecdf` example above (0, 1) we can compare
LPM.CDFs.

```{r lpm-cdf}
LPM(0, 0, x); LPM(0, 1, x)
```

Calculating the probability for every value in $X$, we can plot both methods
visualizing their identical results: `ecdf` function in black and LPM.CDF in
red.

```{r lpm-cdf-plot}
LPM.CDF = LPM(0, sort(x), x)
plot(ecdf(x))
points(sort(x), LPM.CDF, col = 'red')
legend('left', legend = c('ecdf', 'LPM.CDF'), fill = c('black', 'red'), border = NA, bty = 'n')
```

### Degree 1 LPM CDF (LPM.1.CDF)

We already noted how the LPM.CDF is equivalent to the empirical CDF when the
LPM degree is set to zero. However, if we wish to consider the area below the
point when generating a probability, set the degree equal to 1, for any target
($t$) creating LPM.1.CDF.

Degree 0 LPM:

$$LPM(0, t, X) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{n=1}^{N} [\max(t - X_n, 0)]^0$$

Degree 1 LPM:

$$LPM(1, t, X) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{n=1}^{N} [\max(t - X_n, 0)]^1$$

LPM.CDF is equivalent to the following form for any target ($t$) and variable
$X$:

$$\frac{LPM(0, t, X)}{LPM(0, t, X) + UPM(0, t, X)}$$

And LPM.1.CDF is equivalent to the following form for any target ($t$) and
variable $X$:

$$\frac{LPM(1, t, X)}{LPM(1, t, X) + UPM(1, t, X)}$$

Visualizing these CDFs together reveals some interesting properties.

```{r lpm1-cdf}
LPM.CDF = LPM(0, sort(x), x)

# Expanded calculation per equation
LPM.1.CDF = numeric()
for (i in 1:length(x)) {
  LPM.1.CDF[i] = LPM(1, sort(x)[i], x) / (LPM(1, sort(x)[i], x) + UPM(1, sort(x)[i], x))
}

plot(ecdf(x))
points(sort(x), LPM.CDF, col = 'red')
points(sort(x), LPM.1.CDF, col = 'blue')
legend('left', legend = c('ecdf', 'LPM.CDF', 'LPM.1.CDF'), fill = c('black', 'red', 'blue'),
       border = NA, bty = 'n')
```

> **Note (2026).** LPM.1.CDF is the share of deviation area below the target.
> It defines a distribution function of its own, but it is not the frequency
> probability $P(X \le t)$ of the original variable; degree 0 is frequency and
> degree 1 is area (see `examples/example-corrections.md`).

# Comparing to Continuous CDF

R offers the `pnorm` function which returns the integral from $-\infty$ to $x$
where $x$ is a Z-score. Adding this to our previous CDF estimates, we can see
how LPM.1.CDF is more "S" shaped than the others.

```{r pnorm}
plot(ecdf(x))
points(sort(x), LPM.1.CDF, col = 'blue')
points(sort(x), pnorm(sort(x), mean = mean(x), sd = sd(x)), col = 'green')
legend('left', legend = c('ecdf', 'LPM.1.CDF', 'pnorm'), fill = c('black', 'blue', 'green'),
       border = NA, bty = 'n')
```

Extending the number of observations we can see how these functions behave.
The `ecdf` and the `pnorm` are converging while LPM.1.CDF remains distinct:

```{r n1000}
set.seed(123); x = rnorm(1000)
LPM.CDF = LPM(0, sort(x), x)
LPM.1.CDF = LPM.ratio(1, sort(x), x)
plot(ecdf(x))
points(sort(x), LPM.CDF, col = 'red')
points(sort(x), LPM.1.CDF, col = 'blue')
points(sort(x), pnorm(sort(x), mean = mean(x), sd = sd(x)), col = 'green')
legend('left', legend = c('ecdf', 'LPM.CDF', 'LPM.1.CDF', 'pnorm'),
       fill = c('black', 'red', 'blue', 'green'), border = NA, bty = 'n')
```

Even more observations...

```{r n5000}
set.seed(123); x = rnorm(5000)
LPM.CDF = LPM(0, sort(x), x)
LPM.1.CDF = LPM.ratio(1, sort(x), x)
plot(ecdf(x))
points(sort(x), LPM.CDF, col = 'red')
points(sort(x), LPM.1.CDF, col = 'blue')
points(sort(x), pnorm(sort(x), mean = mean(x), sd = sd(x)), col = 'green')
legend('left', legend = c('ecdf', 'LPM.CDF', 'LPM.1.CDF', 'pnorm'),
       fill = c('black', 'red', 'blue', 'green'), border = NA, bty = 'n')
```

# Properties

## Smoothness / Steepness

One property that immediately presents itself is the smoothness of LPM.1.CDF
especially for smaller sample sizes. Remember, this too is an empirical CDF,
however, it is an area based probability and these area considerations are
directly responsible for its distinct smoothness.

Another property is the steepness. This too can be attributed to the LPM.1
being an area based statistic and having the corresponding Logistic growth rate
equal to $e$. Below is a comparison of the discrete LPM.CDF and the continuous
LPM.1.CDF (in black overlayed) with the respective Logistic transformation
growth rates of 1.72 for the Normal approximation, and $e$ (in red).

```{r logistic, message = FALSE}
require(NNS); require(psych)
x = rnorm(10000)

#Logistic growth rate equal to 1.72
curve(logistic(x, a = 1.72), -3, 3, ylab = "Probability of x",
      main = "Logistic transform of x (Logistic growth rate = 1.72)",
      xlab = "z score units", col = 'red', lwd = 3, cex.main = 0.85)

#Redraw for comparison
curve(logistic(x, a = 1.72), -3, 3, ylab = "Probability of x",
      main = "Logistic transform of x (Logistic growth rate = 1.72)
      Black Points of LPM.CDF Overlayed",
      xlab = "z score units", col = 'red', lwd = 3, cex.main = 0.85)

#Discrete Degree 0 LPM CDF
points(sort(x), LPM(0, sort(x), x),
       col = rgb(red = 0, green = 0, blue = 0, alpha = 0.05))

#Logistic growth rate equal to e
curve(logistic(x, a = exp(1)), -3, 3, ylab = "Probability of x",
      main = "Logistic transform of x (Logistic growth rate = e)",
      xlab = "z score units", col = 'red', lwd = 3, cex.main = 0.85)

#Redraw for comparison
curve(logistic(x, a = exp(1)), -3, 3, ylab = "Probability of x",
      main = "Logistic transform of x (Logistic growth rate = e)
      Black Points of LPM.1.CDF Overlayed",
      xlab = "z score units", col = 'red', lwd = 3, cex.main = 0.85)

#Continuous Degree 1 LPM CDF
points(sort(x), LPM.ratio(1, sort(x), x),
       col = rgb(red = 0, green = 0, blue = 0, alpha = 0.05))
```

## Mean Target

For every observation of every type of distribution, LPM.1.CDF is equal to 0.5
when the mean is used as a target.

$$\frac{LPM(1, \mu, X)}{LPM(1, \mu, X) + UPM(1, \mu, X)} = 0.5$$

This bears repeating, "For every observation of every type of distribution".
This is a very special property that can be used to compare means of
distributions without underlying assumptions by using their CDFs, and serves
as the basis of the `NNS.ANOVA` method.

# Distribution Examples

The following examples highlight the LPM.1.CDF stability from a mean target.

## Normal Distribution

```{r normal}
set.seed(123); x = rnorm(100)
LPM.mean_target.CDF = numeric(); LPM.1.mean_target.CDF = numeric()
for (i in 1:length(x)) {
  LPM.mean_target.CDF[i] = LPM(0, mean(x[1:i]), x[1:i])
  LPM.1.mean_target.CDF[i] = LPM.ratio(1, mean(x[1:i]), x[1:i])
}
plot(LPM.mean_target.CDF, col = 'red', type = 'l', lwd = 3)
lines((1:100), LPM.1.mean_target.CDF, col = 'blue', lwd = 3)
legend('topright', legend = c('LPM.CDF', 'LPM.1.CDF'), fill = c('red', 'blue'),
       border = NA, bty = 'n')
```

## Uniform Distribution

```{r uniform}
set.seed(123); x = runif(100)
LPM.mean_target.CDF = numeric(); LPM.1.mean_target.CDF = numeric()
for (i in 1:length(x)) {
  LPM.mean_target.CDF[i] = LPM(0, mean(x[1:i]), x[1:i])
  LPM.1.mean_target.CDF[i] = LPM.ratio(1, mean(x[1:i]), x[1:i])
}
plot(LPM.mean_target.CDF, col = 'red', type = 'l', lwd = 3)
lines((1:100), LPM.1.mean_target.CDF, col = 'blue', lwd = 3)
legend('topright', legend = c('LPM.CDF', 'LPM.1.CDF'), fill = c('red', 'blue'),
       border = NA, bty = 'n')
```

## Poisson Distribution

This example demonstrates the non-association between frequency and area per
the LPM CDFs from a mean target ($\lambda = 1$) in this distribution.

```{r poisson}
set.seed(123); x = rpois(100, lambda = 1)
hist(x)

set.seed(123); x = rpois(100, lambda = 1)
LPM.mean_target.CDF = numeric(); LPM.1.mean_target.CDF = numeric()
for (i in 1:length(x)) {
  LPM.mean_target.CDF[i] = LPM(0, mean(x[1:i]), x[1:i])
  LPM.1.mean_target.CDF[i] = LPM.ratio(1, mean(x[1:i]), x[1:i])
}
plot(LPM.mean_target.CDF, col = 'red', type = 'l', lwd = 3)
lines((1:100), LPM.1.mean_target.CDF, col = 'blue', lwd = 3)
legend('topright', legend = c('LPM.CDF', 'LPM.1.CDF'), fill = c('red', 'blue'),
       border = NA, bty = 'n')
```

# ANOVA Analysis

Using our previously derived information, we can effectively compare two means
and ascertain a degree of certainty [0, 1] whether the difference in means is
zero via their CDFs. This avoids any and all distributional assumptions and
requirements for the underlying data.

## Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS)

The KS statistic measures the maximum distance between the two empirical CDFs
of two given samples in testing whether the samples were drawn from the same
distribution. KS shown in purple below...

```{r ks}
set.seed(123); x = rnorm(100); y = x + .5
plot(ecdf(x), col = 'blue')
lines(ecdf(y), col = 'red')
legend('topleft', legend = c('X', 'Y'), fill = c('blue', 'red'), border = NA, bty = 'n')
cdf1 <- ecdf(x); cdf2 <- ecdf(y)
minMax <- seq(min(x, y), max(x, y), length.out = length(x))
x0 <- minMax[which(abs(cdf1(minMax) - cdf2(minMax)) == max(abs(cdf1(minMax) - cdf2(minMax))))]
y0 <- cdf1(x0)
y1 <- cdf2(x0)
points(c(x0, x0), c(y0, y1), pch = 16, col = "purple")
segments(x0, y0, x0, y1, col = "purple", lty = "dotted", lwd = 2)
```

## NNS.ANOVA

NNS also analyzes the difference in CDFs of the two samples, but it is
performed at the grand mean ($\frac{\mu_x + \mu_y}{2}$) between
distributions, which can be generalized to multiple distributions. This is the
basis for the standard `t.test` comparison.

Further point analysis, including the 12.5, 25, 75 and 87.5 percentile points
coupled with the LPM.1.CDF is what distinguishes `NNS.ANOVA` from `ks.test` in
ascertaining the likelihood the two distributions originated from the same
population.

```{r cdf-plot-function, include = FALSE}
# The comparison figure below is drawn three times.
cdf_compare <- function(x, y) {
  LPM.1.CDF.x = LPM.ratio(1, sort(x), x)
  LPM.1.CDF.y = LPM.ratio(1, sort(y), y)
  plot(sort(x), LPM.1.CDF.x, col = 'blue', type = 'l', lwd = 3,
       xlim = c(min(y), max(y)), xlab = 'X', ylab = "LPM.1.CDF")
  points(sort(y), LPM.1.CDF.y, col = 'red', type = 'l', lwd = 3)
  abline(v = mean(c(mean(x), mean(y))), col = 'darkgrey', lty = 3, lwd = 3)
  target = mean(c(mean(x), mean(y)))
  segments(x0 = min(y), y0 = LPM(1, target, y) / (LPM(1, target, y) + UPM(1, target, y)),
           x1 = target, y1 = LPM(1, target, y) / (LPM(1, target, y) + UPM(1, target, y)),
           col = 'red', lty = 3, lwd = 3)
  segments(x0 = min(y), y0 = LPM(1, target, x) / (LPM(1, target, x) + UPM(1, target, x)),
           x1 = target, y1 = LPM(1, target, x) / (LPM(1, target, x) + UPM(1, target, x)),
           col = 'blue', lty = 3, lwd = 3)
  segments(x0 = min(y), y0 = .5, x1 = target, y1 = .5,
           col = 'darkgrey', lty = 3, lwd = 3)
  #KS line
  lines(ecdf(x), lty = 3, col = 'blue'); lines(ecdf(y), lty = 3, col = 'red')
  cdf1 <- ecdf(x); cdf2 <- ecdf(y)
  minMax <- seq(min(x, y), max(x, y), length.out = length(x))
  x0 <- minMax[which(abs(cdf1(minMax) - cdf2(minMax)) == max(abs(cdf1(minMax) - cdf2(minMax))))]
  y0 <- cdf1(x0)
  y1 <- cdf2(x0)
  points(c(x0, x0), c(y0, y1), pch = 16, col = "purple")
  segments(x0, y0, x0, y1, col = "purple", lty = "dotted")
  legend('topleft', legend = c('X', 'Y'), fill = c('blue', 'red'), border = NA, bty = 'n')
}
```

### Same Population

If both means were equal and the samples were from the same population, the
difference between CDFs at the grand mean (and other percentiles) would be
nil. We know unequivocally that the LPM.1.CDF will equal 0.5 from the mean of a
given sample. Thus two samples with identical means will both have LPM.1.CDF
equal to 0.5 if they are from the same population. The LPM.1.CDF lines are the
thick blue and red lines (for $X$ and $Y$ respectively), while the ECDF lines
for the KS test are the thin lines. (The plotting code is the same in each of
the three cases; it is printed once in the published version's form below.)

```{r same, eval = FALSE}
set.seed(123); x = rnorm(1000); y = rnorm(1000)
# LPM CDFs
LPM.1.CDF.x = LPM.ratio(1, sort(x), x)
LPM.1.CDF.y = LPM.ratio(1, sort(y), y)
# Plot
plot(sort(x), LPM.1.CDF.x, col = 'blue', type = 'l', lwd = 3,
     xlim = c(min(y), max(y)), xlab = 'X', ylab = "LPM.1.CDF")
points(sort(y), LPM.1.CDF.y, col = 'red', type = 'l', lwd = 3)
abline(v = mean(c(mean(x), mean(y))), col = 'darkgrey', lty = 3, lwd = 3)
target = mean(c(mean(x), mean(y)))
segments(x0 = min(y), y0 = LPM(1, target, y) / (LPM(1, target, y) + UPM(1, target, y)),
         x1 = target, y1 = LPM(1, target, y) / (LPM(1, target, y) + UPM(1, target, y)),
         col = 'red', lty = 3, lwd = 3)
segments(x0 = min(y), y0 = LPM(1, target, x) / (LPM(1, target, x) + UPM(1, target, x)),
         x1 = target, y1 = LPM(1, target, x) / (LPM(1, target, x) + UPM(1, target, x)),
         col = 'blue', lty = 3, lwd = 3)
segments(x0 = min(y), y0 = .5, x1 = target, y1 = .5,
         col = 'darkgrey', lty = 3, lwd = 3)
#KS line
lines(ecdf(x), lty = 3, col = 'blue'); lines(ecdf(y), lty = 3, col = 'red')
cdf1 <- ecdf(x); cdf2 <- ecdf(y)
minMax <- seq(min(x, y), max(x, y), length.out = length(x))
x0 <- minMax[which(abs(cdf1(minMax) - cdf2(minMax)) == max(abs(cdf1(minMax) - cdf2(minMax))))]
y0 <- cdf1(x0)
y1 <- cdf2(x0)
points(c(x0, x0), c(y0, y1), pch = 16, col = "purple")
segments(x0, y0, x0, y1, col = "purple", lty = "dotted")
legend('topleft', legend = c('X', 'Y'), fill = c('blue', 'red'), border = NA, bty = 'n')
```

```{r same-run, echo = FALSE}
set.seed(123); x = rnorm(1000); y = rnorm(1000)
cdf_compare(x, y)
```

Comparing NNS CDF analysis (degree of certainty of the null hypothesis that the
difference in means is zero) with a t-test (and its infamous p-value) and a
ks.test:

```{r same-tests}
NNS.ANOVA(x, y, means.only = TRUE)$Certainty
t.test(x, y)
NNS.ANOVA(x, y, means.only = FALSE, plot = FALSE)$Certainty
ks.test(x, y)
```

### Different Populations

If both means were equal and the samples were from different populations, the
difference between CDFs at the grand mean would be evident.

```{r different}
set.seed(123); x = rnorm(1000); y = rnorm(1000, sd = 3)
cdf_compare(x, y)
```

Comparing NNS CDF analysis with a t-test and a KS-test:

```{r different-tests}
NNS.ANOVA(x, y, means.only = TRUE)$Certainty
t.test(x, y)
NNS.ANOVA(x, y, means.only = FALSE, plot = FALSE)$Certainty
ks.test(x, y)
```

### VERY Different Populations

Note the difference between the NNS certainty vs. the t-test p-value...

```{r very-different}
set.seed(123); x = rnorm(1000); y = rnorm(1000, sd = 10)
cdf_compare(x, y)
```

Comparing NNS CDF analysis with a t-test and KS-test:

```{r very-different-tests}
NNS.ANOVA(x, y, means.only = TRUE)$Certainty
t.test(x, y)
NNS.ANOVA(x, y, means.only = FALSE, plot = FALSE)$Certainty
ks.test(x, y)
```

Of course t-tests are only informed by differences in means, while NNS and KS
consider variances and other distribution characteristics. However, as we see,
KS can evaluate differences far removed from the means while NNS simultaneously
considers sample means explicitly.

# NNS Certainties

Finally a note on the NNS certainty statistic. NNS uses the squared sum of
absolute LPM.1.CDF deviations from the 0.5 null hypothesis. The range of these
deviations is [0, .5] (representing a target below the sample range and above
the sample range respectively). The associated certainties over the range of
possible deviations is clearly bound within the interval [0, 1].

```{r certainty-curve}
deviation = seq(.01, .5, .01)
plot(deviation, (0.5 - deviation)^2 / .25, type = 'l',
     lwd = 4, xlab = "Deviation", ylab = "NNS certainty")
```

> **Note (2026).** NNS certainty is a descriptive agreement score for the
> selected target. It is not a calibrated probability and not a p-value, so the
> comparisons below describe how the two quantities behave in these
> simulations rather than error rates (see `examples/example-corrections.md`).

## NNS Certainties vs. p-values

Below is a visualization of the stability of the NNS certainty statistic vs.
the corresponding p-value of the t-test and KS test. The first example creates
two standard normal distributions ranging in size from 5 to 500 observations.

```{r stability-1, warning = FALSE}
ks.certainties = numeric(); ks.p.values = numeric()
t.certainties = numeric(); t.p.values = numeric()

for (i in 5:500) {
  set.seed(123)
  x1 = rnorm(i); x2 = rnorm(i)
  ks.certainties[i] = NNS.ANOVA(x1, x2, plot = FALSE, means.only = FALSE)$Certainty
  ks.p.values[i] = ks.test(x1, x2)$p.value
  t.certainties[i] = NNS.ANOVA(x1, x2, plot = FALSE, means.only = TRUE)$Certainty
  t.p.values[i] = t.test(x1, x2)$p.value
}
```

### t.test

```{r stability-1-t}
plot(t.certainties, pch = 19, xlab = 'n', ylab = "CV (Black) p.value (Red)",
     col = rgb(red = 0, green = 0, blue = 0, alpha = .5), ylim = c(0, 1))
points(t.p.values,
       col = rgb(red = 1, green = 0, blue = 0, alpha = .5), pch = 19)
abline(h = 0.05, col = 'purple')
```

### ks.test

```{r stability-1-ks}
plot(ks.certainties, pch = 19, xlab = 'n', ylab = "CV (Black) p.value (Red)",
     col = rgb(red = 0, green = 0, blue = 0, alpha = .5), ylim = c(0, 1))
points(ks.p.values,
       col = rgb(red = 1, green = 0, blue = 0, alpha = .5), pch = 19)
abline(h = 0.05, col = 'purple')
```

Finally, we isolate a single distribution and increase the number of
observations from 5 to 500. Again, note the stability of the NNS certainty
statistic...

```{r stability-2, warning = FALSE}
ks.certainties = numeric(); ks.p.values = numeric()
t.certainties = numeric(); t.p.values = numeric()

set.seed(123)
x1 = rnorm(500); x2 = rnorm(500)

for (i in 5:500) {
  ks.certainties[i] = NNS.ANOVA(x1[1:i], x2[1:i], plot = FALSE, means.only = FALSE)$Certainty
  ks.p.values[i] = ks.test(x1[1:i], x2[1:i])$p.value
  t.certainties[i] = NNS.ANOVA(x1[1:i], x2[1:i], plot = FALSE, means.only = TRUE)$Certainty
  t.p.values[i] = t.test(x1[1:i], x2[1:i])$p.value
}
```

### t.test

```{r stability-2-t}
plot(t.certainties, pch = 19, xlab = 'n', ylab = "CV (Black) p.value (Red)",
     col = rgb(red = 0, green = 0, blue = 0, alpha = .5), ylim = c(0, 1))
points(t.p.values,
       col = rgb(red = 1, green = 0, blue = 0, alpha = .5), pch = 19)
abline(h = 0.05, col = 'purple')
```

### ks.test

```{r stability-2-ks}
plot(ks.certainties, pch = 19, xlab = 'n', ylab = "CV (Black) p.value (Red)",
     col = rgb(red = 0, green = 0, blue = 0, alpha = .5), ylim = c(0, 1))
points(ks.p.values,
       col = rgb(red = 1, green = 0, blue = 0, alpha = .5), pch = 19)
abline(h = 0.05, col = 'purple')
```

# NNS Certainties vs. p-values and the role of 'Power'

One obvious culprit for the difference in NNS certainties and KS test p-values
is the power, or probability of a type II error. From the critical $\alpha$
level selected ($\alpha = 0.05$) in the reference distribution ($X_1$), we can
easily calculate the probability below this level of the other sampled
distribution ($X_2$).

For instance, if the sample mean of $X_2$ is greater than the mean of $X_1$,
the $\beta$ is simply the LPM.0.CDF of $X_2$ from this $\alpha$ target, defined
in section 2.1.1. Thus, the $(1 - \beta)$ power measure is the UPM.0.CDF of
$X_2$ from this target. Stated more clearly, the UPM.0.CDF is the probability
above a target in a distribution.

Let's demonstrate the role of power in both tests' assessment of the
significance in the difference of distributions. We will keep one sample
$N(0, 1)$ as our reference distribution $X_1$, and sample another distribution
with an increasing mean from 0:4 by increments of 0.01, $X_2$.

We will then compute the associated $\beta$ for $X_2$ at $\alpha = 0.05$ and
determine the correlation between NNS certainties and p-values to this $\beta$
value (we are using the empirical 5% $\alpha$ level, not the standard z score
of 1.645, even though our results do not differ materially). As $\beta$
decreases, the power increases and the NNS certainty and KS test p-value
should decrease as well...

```{r power, warning = FALSE}
certainties = numeric(); p.values = numeric(); betas = numeric()

set.seed(123)
x1 = rnorm(500, mean = 0, sd = 1)

# alpha = 0.05 in X1
alpha = UPM.VaR(.95, 0, x1)

for (i in seq(0, 4, .01)) {
  set.seed(123)
  x2 = rnorm(500, mean = i, sd = 1)
  certainties[which(i == seq(0, 4, .01))] = NNS.ANOVA(x1, x2, plot = FALSE, means.only = FALSE)$Certainty
  p.values[which(i == seq(0, 4, .01))] = ks.test(x1, x2)$p.value
  betas[which(i == seq(0, 4, .01))] = LPM(0, 1.645, x2)
}

plot(seq(0, 4, .01), certainties, pch = 19, ylab = "CV (Black) p.value (Red) Betas (Blue)",
     ylim = c(0, 1), xlab = "Difference in means",
     col = rgb(red = 0, green = 0, blue = 0, alpha = 0.5))
points(seq(0, 4, .01), p.values,
       col = rgb(red = 1, green = 0, blue = 0, alpha = 0.5), pch = 19)
points(seq(0, 4, .01), betas,
       col = rgb(red = 0, green = 0, blue = 1, alpha = 0.5), pch = 19)
abline(h = 0.2, col = 'purple')
```

We can visualize how the power increases (via decreasing $\beta$) and indeed
NNS certainties and p-values decrease. What is concerning however, is the rate
at which the p-values decrease. The purple horizontal line highlights 0.2, and
$\beta < 0.2$ translates to a power greater than 80%. Why does the p-value
completely ignore the power of the test? NNS certainty does a much better job
of conveying this information.

## Power Correlations

Using a linear correlation measure, we quantify the relationship between
$\beta$ and the two measures of significance in the difference of means:

```{r power-correlations}
cor(betas, p.values)
cor(betas, certainties)
```

In the published version, NNS certainty had a much stronger correlation to
the power of the test than the p-value (0.676 against 0.285). Given the
relevant power information, are KS test p-values too hastily declaring a
significant difference in distributions?

## Confidence Intervals

The 95% confidence interval of the mean of $X_1$ spans the interval
[-1.96, 1.96]. Given this range, how certain can we be of a difference in means
of two normally distributed unit variance distributions equal to 0.5 being
significantly different? In fact, if we reverse the procedure and ask: What
percentage confidence interval does a difference in means of 0.5 represent?,
we get an alarming result. We use the `uniroot` command in R to find the
associated percentage of the `qnorm` value representing a $\pm 0.5$ difference
in means between two distributions.

```{r uniroot}
f = function(x) qnorm(x, mean = 0, sd = 1) + .5
uniroot(f, tol = 0.0001, c(.3, .5))
```

Our result shows that a difference in means of 0.5 has an associated
confidence interval of 61.70846% on our reference distribution $X_1$. The KS
test p-value is significant at a much lower difference in means, ignoring the
much lower confidence interval.

> **Note (2026).** The interval [-1.96, 1.96] and the 61.7% figure describe a
> single draw from $N(0, 1)$. The sampling uncertainty of a difference in means
> of two samples of 500 has standard deviation $\sqrt{2/500} \approx 0.063$,
> so a difference of 0.5 is about eight standard errors; a test of whether two
> samples come from the same distribution is answering that second question.

# Remarks

In summary, the well documented shortfalls of the p-value are warranted. It is
a test that ignores too much information regarding the power of the test and
the associated confidence interval of the difference in means. NNS certainty
captures this information with its use of CDFs based on partial moments.

This is merely an introductory work and by no means exhaustive. A further
discussion comparing the underlying assumptions to p-values to that of NNS is
presented in the References section.
